Harar Jugol is the old walled city of Harar, on a hilltop in eastern Ethiopia. Its wall, the Jugol, was built in the 1550s, and the city inside is crowded with more than eighty mosques and a hundred shrines. It is often called the fourth holy city of Islam, a claim made locally.

Harar was the capital of the Adal Sultanate. From here Ahmad ibn Ibrahim, known as Gragn, led the jihad that nearly overran Christian Ethiopia in the 1530s. After his death the emir Nur ibn Mujahid built the wall, with five gates, against attacks by the Oromo and others.

For three centuries Harar was an independent emirate, a centre of Islamic learning and a market for coffee, khat and cloth, with its own Harari language. In 1887 Menelik II conquered it and brought it into the Ethiopian empire. The French poet Arthur Rimbaud traded there in the 1880s. The old town became a World Heritage Site in 2006.
